claim: C. trachomatis grows in a glycogen-rich vacuole
source: The human pathogen Chlamydia trachomatis grows in a glycogen-rich vacuole.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of C. trachomatis

claim: Host glycogen stores shift to the vacuole through bulk uptake from the cytoplasmic pool
source: We reveal that host glycogen stores shift to the vacuole through two pathways: bulk uptake from the cytoplasmic pool, and de novo synthesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: Host glycogen stores shift to the vacuole through de novo synthesis
source: We reveal that host glycogen stores shift to the vacuole through two pathways: bulk uptake from the cytoplasmic pool, and de novo synthesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: Bacterial glycogen metabolism enzymes are secreted into the vacuole lumen through type 3 secretion
source: We provide evidence that bacterial glycogen metabolism enzymes are secreted into the vacuole lumen through type 3 secretion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by heterologous secretion assays and immunofluorescence data

claim: Bacteria co-opt the host transporter SLC35D2 to import UDP-glucose into the vacuole
source: Our data bring strong support to the following scenario: bacteria co-opt the host transporter SLC35D2 to import UDP-glucose into the vacuole, where it serves as substrate for de novo glycogen synthesis, through a remarkable adaptation of the bacterial glycogen synthase.
evidence: This is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments showing reduced glycogen accumulation and localization of SLC35D2-HA to the inclusion membrane

claim: UDP-glucose serves as substrate for de novo glycogen synthesis in the vacuole
source: Our data bring strong support to the following scenario: bacteria co-opt the host transporter SLC35D2 to import UDP-glucose into the vacuole, where it serves as substrate for de novo glycogen synthesis, through a remarkable adaptation of the bacterial glycogen synthase.
evidence: This is supported by UGP2 knockdown experiments and zymogram analysis showing GlgA activity on UDP-Glc

claim: Chlamydial glycogen synthase shows remarkable adaptation in substrate specificity
source: Our data bring strong support to the following scenario: bacteria co-opt the host transporter SLC35D2 to import UDP-glucose into the vacuole, where it serves as substrate for de novo glycogen synthesis, through a remarkable adaptation of the bacterial glycogen synthase.
evidence: This is supported by zymogram analysis showing C. trachomatis GlgA can use both UDP-Glc and ADP-Glc, unlike E. coli GlgA

claim: Parasitophorous vacuoles provide a microorganism-controlled metabolically active compartment essential for redirecting host resources to the pathogens
source: Based on these findings we propose that parasitophorous vacuoles not only offer protection but also provide a microorganism-controlled metabolically active compartment essential for redirecting host resources to the pathogens.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about glycogen metabolism in the inclusion

claim: Residence in a vacuole provides shelter against cytosolic host defense
source: One recognized advantage of a vacuole is that it provides a shelter against cytosolic host defense (Kumar and Valdivia, 2009), to the cost of limited access to cytosolic nutrients.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: Residence in a vacuole limits access to cytosolic nutrients
source: One recognized advantage of a vacuole is that it provides a shelter against cytosolic host defense (Kumar and Valdivia, 2009), to the cost of limited access to cytosolic nutrients.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: C. trachomatis is the leading cause of infectious blindness
source: The human adapted strain C. trachomatis is the leading cause of infectious blindness (Taylor et al., 2014) as well as of sexually transmitted infections caused by bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: C. trachomatis is the leading cause of sexually transmitted infections caused by bacteria
source: The human adapted strain C. trachomatis is the leading cause of infectious blindness (Taylor et al., 2014) as well as of sexually transmitted infections caused by bacteria.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: C. trachomatis displays a genome reduced to around one million base pairs
source: C. trachomatis displays a genome reduced to around one million base pairs and therefore highly relies on the host with regard to several essential metabolic pathways, such as nucleotide or amino acid biosynthesis (Stephens et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: C. trachomatis highly relies on the host for nucleotide biosynthesis
source: C. trachomatis displays a genome reduced to around one million base pairs and therefore highly relies on the host with regard to several essential metabolic pathways, such as nucleotide or amino acid biosynthesis (Stephens et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: C. trachomatis highly relies on the host for amino acid biosynthesis
source: C. trachomatis displays a genome reduced to around one million base pairs and therefore highly relies on the host with regard to several essential metabolic pathways, such as nucleotide or amino acid biosynthesis (Stephens et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: Lipid droplets have been observed in the inclusion lumen
source: Lipid droplets and peroxisomes have been observed in the inclusion lumen, indicating that this compartment is able to engulf large particles to meet bacterial needs (Boncompain et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work

claim: Peroxisomes have been observed in the inclusion lumen
source: Lipid droplets and peroxisomes have been observed in the inclusion lumen, indicating that this compartment is able to engulf large particles to meet bacterial needs (Boncompain et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work

claim: The inclusion compartment is able to engulf large particles to meet bacterial needs
source: Lipid droplets and peroxisomes have been observed in the inclusion lumen, indicating that this compartment is able to engulf large particles to meet bacterial needs (Boncompain et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of large particles in the inclusion lumen

claim: C. trachomatis and C. muridarum are unique amongst Chlamydiae for their ability to accumulate glucose under the form of glycogen in the inclusion lumen
source: C. trachomatis, and the closely related mouse and hamster pathogen C. muridarum, are unique amongst Chlamydiae for their ability to accumulate glucose (Glc) under the form of glycogen in the inclusion lumen (Gordon and Quan, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: Glucose deprivation leads to a complete loss of infectivity in C. trachomatis
source: Glc deprivation leads to a complete loss of infectivity (Harper et al., 2000; Iliffe-Lee and McClarty, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work

claim: The C. trachomatis genome encodes for all the enzymes necessary for a functional glycogenesis and glycogenolysis
source: The C. trachomatis genome encodes for all the enzymes necessary for a functional glycogenesis and glycogenolysis (Stephens et al., 1998) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: Other Chlamydia species have a complete set of glycogen metabolism enzymes despite not accumulating glycogen in the inclusion
source: Although they do not accumulate glycogen in the inclusion, other Chlamydia species also have a complete set of those enzymes, a surprising observation given that this pathway is absent in most intracellular bacteria (Henrissat et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: The glycogen metabolism pathway is absent in most intracellular bacteria
source: Although they do not accumulate glycogen in the inclusion, other Chlamydia species also have a complete set of those enzymes, a surprising observation given that this pathway is absent in most intracellular bacteria (Henrissat et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: Pathogenic Chlamydiae lack a hexokinase
source: Intriguingly, pathogenic Chlamydiae lack a hexokinase, the enzyme phosphorylating Glc, and therefore rely on the import of phosphorylated sugars for glycolysis or glycogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of pathogenic Chlamydiae

claim: Pathogenic Chlamydiae rely on the import of phosphorylated sugars for glycolysis or glycogenesis
source: Intriguingly, pathogenic Chlamydiae lack a hexokinase, the enzyme phosphorylating Glc, and therefore rely on the import of phosphorylated sugars for glycolysis or glycogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of hexokinase

claim: Loss of the C. trachomatis plasmid is associated with decreased GlgA expression
source: Finally, the very large majority of circulating C. trachomatis strains contain a 7.5 kb plasmid. Loss of this plasmid is associated with decreased GlgA expression and impaired glycogen accumulation (Carlson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: Loss of the C. trachomatis plasmid is associated with impaired glycogen accumulation
source: Finally, the very large majority of circulating C. trachomatis strains contain a 7.5 kb plasmid. Loss of this plasmid is associated with decreased GlgA expression and impaired glycogen accumulation (Carlson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: Glycogen is detected in the inclusion lumen and within EBs by TEM
source: We used transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to determine more precisely its subcellular localization and detected the polysaccharide in two locations: in the inclusion lumen, and within EBs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in TEM images shown in Figure 1B

claim: Glycogen was not observed in RBs
source: We did not observe glycogen in RBs, in contrast to an earlier report (Chiappino et al., 1995).
evidence: This is based on TEM observations in this study

claim: Intraluminal glycogen deposits are physically larger than cytoplasmic glycogen
source: Intraluminal glycogen deposits are physically larger than in the cytoplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in TEM images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Glycogen in the inclusion lumen does not result from the release of bacterial stores
source: This experiment demonstrates that glycogen in the inclusion lumen does not result from the release of bacterial stores.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the glucose deprivation and restoration experiment shown in Figure 1C,D

claim: Luminal glycogen first appeared between 16 and 20 hpi
source: The kinetics of glycogen appearance in the inclusion was carefully examined next by TEM. Luminal glycogen first appeared between 16 and 20 hpi (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and was abundant 24 hpi.
evidence: This is observed in the time course TEM analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Luminal glycogen deposit takes place at a time when RBs largely predominate over EBs
source: Thus, luminal glycogen deposit took place at a time when RBs largely predominate over EBs.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of glycogen appearance (16-20 hpi) and knowledge of the developmental cycle

claim: The process of glycogen accumulation in the inclusion is initiated by RBs
source: This observation suggests that, while glycogen accumulation in the inclusion is most obvious at later stages of infection, when EBs accumulate, the process is initiated by RBs.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of glycogen appearance when RBs predominate

claim: Host glycogen synthase Gys1 accumulates within the inclusion lumen
source: Gys1, the host glycogen synthase, produces linear chains of Glc and is tightly bound to glycogen (Luck, 1961; Stapleton et al., 2010). Gys1 staining with specific antibodies gave a patchy pattern in the cytoplasm, as expected since it mirrors the distribution of glycogen. In addition, we observed that the enzyme accumulated within the inclusion lumen.
evidence: This is observed by immunofluorescence with anti-Gys1 antibodies

claim: Gys1 staining in the inclusion lumen is specific and not a post-fixation artifact
source: Staining was specific since it disappeared when Gys1 expression was knocked down using siRNA prior to infection (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiment shown in Figure 2A

claim: Gys1 appearance in the inclusion lumen requires the presence of host glycogen
source: When we deprived the cells of Glc for two days before infection, and thus decreased cytoplasmic glycogen, Gys1 staining in the inclusion lumen was considerably reduced, while remaining abundant in the cytoplasm. This observation shows that Gys1 appearance in the inclusion lumen requires the presence of host glycogen, and is likely not the result of a post-fixation artifact. (Figure 2—figure supplement1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by glucose deprivation experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Glycogen-filled vesicular structures are observed in the inclusion lumen
source: TEM observations also came in support of this scenario, since we could observe one or more glycogen-filled vesicular structures in the inclusion lumen of about 20% of the glycogen-positive inclusions we examined (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly observed in TEM images shown in Figure 2B

claim: The pathway of bulk host glycogen uptake is independent of autophagy
source: Inclusions of Atg5-/- MEFs still harboured glycogen, Gys1 and glycogen-filled vesicles, demonstrating that the pathway of bulk host glycogen uptake is independent of autophagy (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Atg5-/- cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Knocking down Gys1 expression did not abolish glycogen accumulation in the inclusions
source: However, knocking down Gys1 expression did not abolish glycogen accumulation in the inclusions (Figure 2D, bottom).
evidence: This is observed in PAS staining after Gys1 knockdown shown in Figure 2D

claim: Inclusions of cells treated with siRNA against Gys1 contained 82% of the glycogen measured in cells treated with control siRNA
source: We measured the pixel intensity of the PAS staining in inclusions 48 hpi, and used inclusion staining of cells infected in the absence of Glc to determine the background level, which we subtracted. Inclusions of cells treated with siRNA against Gys1 contained 82% (s.e.m. 4.9) of the glycogen measured in cells treated with control siRNA.
evidence: This is quantified from PAS staining intensity measurements

claim: De novo glycogen synthesis takes place in the inclusion lumen
source: This experiment strongly suggested that bulk import of host glycogen was at least partially responsible for intraluminal glycogen accumulation. However, it did not appear to be the main contributor and indicated that de novo glycogen synthesis in the inclusion lumen also took place.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of glycogen after Gys1 knockdown

claim: glgA transcription was delayed until 16 hpi
source: For most proteins, RNA levels increased between 8 and 24 hpi, mirroring the known increase in bacterial metabolic activity in this time window (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). glgA stood out, as its transcription was delayed until 16 hpi.
evidence: This is observed in qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: glgA expression correlates with the timing of glycogen appearance in the inclusion lumen
source: glgA expression thus correlates very well with the timing of glycogen appearance in the inclusion lumen, between 16 and 20 hpi, implicating that the enzyme might be involved in luminal glycogen synthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between glgA transcription timing and glycogen appearance

claim: Secretion of GlgA into the inclusion lumen has been demonstrated
source: Indeed, secretion of GlgA into the inclusion lumen, as well as into the host cytoplasm, has recently been demonstrated (Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: A GlgB mutant strain shows massive precipitation of glycogen in the inclusion
source: In addition, a GlgB mutant strain shows massive precipitation of glycogen in the inclusion (Nguyen and Valdivia, 2012), due to accumulation of unbranched glycogen, implicating that GlgB normally functions in the inclusion lumen.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: GlgX is found in the inclusion lumen with mostly no overlap with bacteria
source: In cells infected for 24 hpi or 48 hpi, GlgX was found in the inclusion lumen, with mostly no overlap with bacteria, demonstrating secretion within the inclusion lumen (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3A

claim: GlgX was detected on the inclusion membrane 24 hpi, but not 48 hpi
source: Interestingly, GlgX was also detected on the inclusion membrane 24 hpi, but not 48 hpi (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Five out of six glycogen metabolism enzyme chimeras (GlgA/Cya, GlgB/Cya, GlgX/Cya, GlgP/Cya and MalQ/Cya) were secreted in the Shigella T3S assay
source: Five out of the six chimera tested, GlgA/Cya, GlgB/Cya, GlgX/Cya, GlgP/Cya and MalQ/Cya, were secreted in the supernatant of cultures when transformed in a S. flexneri mutant with constitutive T3S (ipaB strain), and not when transformed in a mutant deficient for T3S (mxiD strain).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the heterologous secretion assay shown in Figure 3B

claim: GlgC/Cya was not detected in the culture supernatant, suggesting GlgC is not a substrate of T3S
source: The sixth chimera tested, GlgC/Cya, was not detected in the culture supernatant, suggesting that GlgC, which converts Glc1P into ADP-Glc, is not a substrate of T3S (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the heterologous secretion assay shown in Figure 3B

claim: Only [C14]-Glc6P was taken up by purified EBs
source: We investigated what form of Glc the bacteria are able to take up by incubating purified EBs with radioactively labeled [C14]-Glc, [C14]-Glc1P or [C14]-Glc6P, in absence or presence of a 50-fold excess of non-radioactive Glc, Glc1P or Glc6P. Only [C14]-Glc6P was taken up by bacteria, and only Glc6P could compete it out (Figure 4A), demonstrating that the uptake was saturable, as expected for a transporter.
evidence: This is demonstrated by radioactive uptake assay shown in Figure 4A

claim: C. trachomatis MrsA contains a functional T3S signal
source: Using the heterologous test of secretion we found that C. trachomatis MrsA contains a functional T3S signal (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the heterologous secretion assay shown in Figure 4B

claim: Transfection of cells with flag-tagged chlamydial GlgA led to massive glycogen accumulation
source: Transfection of cells with flag-tagged chlamydial GlgA led to massive glycogen accumulation, proving that indeed C. trachomatis GlgA is functional on UDP-Glc (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PAS staining of transfected cells shown in Figure 5A

claim: C. trachomatis GlgA is functional on UDP-Glc
source: Transfection of cells with flag-tagged chlamydial GlgA led to massive glycogen accumulation, proving that indeed C. trachomatis GlgA is functional on UDP-Glc (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by glycogen accumulation in transfected cells where only UDP-Glc is available

claim: E. coli GlgA showed activity exclusively upon incubation with ADP-Glc
source: While E. coli GlgA showed activity exclusively upon incubation with ADP-Glc, as expected, the chlamydial GlgA showed activity with both substrates (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by zymogram analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Chlamydial GlgA showed activity with both UDP-Glc and ADP-Glc
source: While E. coli GlgA showed activity exclusively upon incubation with ADP-Glc, as expected, the chlamydial GlgA showed activity with both substrates (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by zymogram analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Glycogen accumulation within the inclusion lumen decreased to 57% in cells treated with siRNA against UGP2 compared to cells treated with control siRNA
source: We measured the pixel intensity of the PAS staining in inclusions as described above. Glycogen accumulation within the inclusion lumen decreased to 57% (s.e.m. = 5.8) in cells treated with a siRNA against UGP2 compared to cells treated with control siRNA (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is quantified from PAS staining after UGP2 knockdown shown in Figure 5C,D

claim: UDP-Glc is the substrate for sugar import into the inclusion
source: These data strongly argue for UDP-Glc being the substrate for sugar import into the inclusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the UGP2 knockdown results and GlgA substrate specificity

claim: SLC35D2 was experimentally shown to be able to transport UDP-Glc
source: Among the large family of annotated human sugar transporters, only SLC35D2 was experimentally shown to be able to transport UDP-Glc (Suda et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: SLC35D2-HA was enriched around the inclusion in infected cells
source: In cells infected with C. trachomatis, a construct of the transporter bearing a C-terminal HA-tag was enriched around the inclusion (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is observed by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 6A

claim: SLC35D2 is present on the inclusion membrane
source: By TEM, we detected the presence of the transporter on the inclusion membrane (Figure 6B). Staining was specific since we observed 0.96 gold particles per μm of inclusion membrane examined, against 0.12 gold particles per μm in non-transfected cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immuno-EM shown in Figure 6B

claim: Glycogen accumulation in the inclusion decreased to 43% when SLC35D2 was silenced
source: To test this hypothesis we silenced SLC35D2 expression using siRNA prior to infection. In these conditions, glycogen accumulation in the inclusion decreased to 43% (s.e.m. = 1.7) (Figure 6C,D), thus to a level similar to that when UGP2 had been silenced (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is quantified from PAS staining after SLC35D2 knockdown shown in Figure 6C,D

claim: C. trachomatis co-opts the host nucleotide-sugar transporter SLC35D2 to favor UDP-Glc import into the inclusion lumen
source: These data strongly suggest that C. trachomatis co-opts the host nucleotide-sugar transporter to favor UDP-Glc import into the inclusion lumen.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization of SLC35D2 to the inclusion membrane and the effect of its knockdown on glycogen accumulation

claim: Additional Gys1 depletion did not decrease luminal glycogen content further than what SLC35D2 depletion did
source: We depleted Gys1 and SLC35D2 for 48 hr before infecting the cells, and applied PAS staining 48 hr after infection. Additional Gys1 depletion did not decrease luminal glycogen content further than what SLC35D2 depletion did, confirming that in C. trachomatis infected cells bulk import of cytoplasmic glycogen plays only a minor part in intraluminal glycogen accumulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by double knockdown experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: Bulk import of cytoplasmic glycogen plays only a minor part in intraluminal glycogen accumulation in C. trachomatis infected cells
source: Additional Gys1 depletion did not decrease luminal glycogen content further than what SLC35D2 depletion did, confirming that in C. trachomatis infected cells bulk import of cytoplasmic glycogen plays only a minor part in intraluminal glycogen accumulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the double knockdown experiment results

claim: Decrease in progeny was never more than two-fold when both Gys1 and SLC35D2 were depleted simultaneously
source: We measured the consequences on progeny 30 hpi to minimize the effect of SLC35D2 depletion on cell viability that we observed in some experiments. Decrease in progeny was never more than two-fold, indicating that even when both Gys1 and SLC35D2 were depleted simultaneously, there was no severe impact on bacterial development (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is measured by reinfection assay shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: C. muridarum mutants P2B10 and P3B4 carry mutations in conserved residues of GlgA
source: We selected two clones, P2B10 and P3B4, which carry mutations in conserved residues of GlgA (H131Y for P2B10 and G386E for P3B4), suggesting that they may have a strong, if not complete, loss of function (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the alignment in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: Glycogen accumulation in P2B10 and P3B4 inclusions 48 hpi was reduced to 40 and 51% respectively of its level in the parental strain
source: Glycogen accumulation in P2B10 and P3B4 inclusions 48 hpi was reduced to 40 and 51% respectively of its level in the parental strain (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is quantified from PAS staining shown in Figure 7A

claim: Progeny was reduced 7-fold and 3-fold in P2B10 and P3B4 respectively
source: Impact on infectivity was assessed by collecting the bacteria 48 hpi, and re-infecting fresh HeLa cells. Progeny was reduced 7-fold and 3-fold in P2B10 and P3B4 respectively, demonstrating that a defect in GlgA results in an impaired infectivity in vitro (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is measured by reinfection assay shown in Figure 7B

claim: A defect in GlgA results in impaired infectivity in vitro
source: Progeny was reduced 7-fold and 3-fold in P2B10 and P3B4 respectively, demonstrating that a defect in GlgA results in an impaired infectivity in vitro (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reduced progeny of GlgA mutants shown in Figure 7B

claim: In the parental C. muridarum strain, depletion of Gys1 reduced glycogen accumulation by 29%
source: In the parental strain, depletion of Gys1 reduced glycogen accumulation by 29%, similar to C. trachomatis reduction (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is quantified from PAS staining after Gys1 knockdown shown in Figure 7A

claim: In the GlgA mutants, depletion of Gys1 also decreased glycogen accumulation
source: In the mutants, depletion of Gys1 also decreased glycogen accumulation, demonstrating that part of the residual glycogen observed in the mutants is due to bulk glycogen import.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 7A

claim: Part of the residual glycogen observed in the GlgA mutants is due to bulk glycogen import
source: In the mutants, depletion of Gys1 also decreased glycogen accumulation, demonstrating that part of the residual glycogen observed in the mutants is due to bulk glycogen import.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of Gys1 depletion in the mutants

claim: Decreasing luminal glycogen further by silencing Gys1 expression did not have a higher impact on the progeny of the mutants than it had on the parental strain
source: Interestingly, decreasing luminal glycogen further by silencing Gys1 expression content did not have a higher impact on the progeny of the mutants than it had on the parental strain, rather less so (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is observed in the reinfection assay shown in Figure 7B

claim: In the P2B10 mutant, the defect in progeny is mostly due to a deficiency in bacterial glycogen synthesis rather than in luminal glycogen storage
source: In particular, Gys1 depletion did not decrease progeny of the P2B10 mutant. This observation suggests that in this mutant, the defect in progeny is mostly due to a deficiency in bacterial glycogen synthesis rather than in luminal glycogen storage.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of Gys1 depletion on P2B10 progeny

claim: Two independent processes contribute to glycogen accumulation in the C. trachomatis inclusion lumen: bulk uptake from the host cytoplasm and de novo synthesis
source: This work shows that two independent processes contribute to glycogen accumulation in the C. trachomatis inclusion lumen: bulk uptake from the host cytoplasm and de novo synthesis (Figure 8).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the work, supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript

claim: Intraluminal glycogen accumulation had previously been thought to be due to bacterial lysis and release of chlamydial glycogen
source: Intraluminal glycogen accumulation had previously been thought to be due to bacterial lysis and to the release of chlamydial glycogen into the surrounding environment (Chiappino et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a previous hypothesis cited from the literature

claim: Glycogen appears first in the inclusion lumen and only later in EBs
source: In the present work we observed that glycogen appears first in the inclusion lumen and only later in EBs.
evidence: This is observed in the time course experiments

claim: Bacterial lysis is not the source of luminal glycogen
source: Thus, bacterial lysis is not the source of luminal glycogen.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of glycogen appearance

claim: The host enzyme Gys1 is translocated into the vacuole
source: First, the host enzyme Gys1, which is known to bind to glycogen (Roach et al., 2012), is translocated into the vacuole, arguing for uptake of host glycogen in bulk.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence showing Gys1 in the inclusion lumen

claim: Depleting cytoplasmic glycogen by silencing Gys1 partially reduced luminal glycogen content in C. trachomatis and C. muridarum
source: Finally, depleting cytoplasmic glycogen by silencing Gys1 partially reduced luminal glycogen content in C. trachomatis and C. muridarum.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Gys1 knockdown experiments

claim: Translocation of cytoplasmic glycogen confirms the ability for the inclusion to take up large particles from the host cytoplasm
source: Translocation of cytoplasmic glycogen confirms the ability for the inclusion to take up large particles from the host cytoplasm, already illustrated with the uptake of lipid droplets and peroxisomes (Boncompain et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the current findings and previous work on lipid droplets and peroxisomes

claim: Uptake of large particles likely occurs through invagination of the inclusion membrane
source: This likely occurs through invagination of the inclusion membrane, but the underlying mechanisms remains to be investigated.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation of vesicular structures

claim: Multi-layered glycogen-filled vesicles do not originate from an Atg5-dependent autophagic process
source: While multi-layered glycogen-filled vesicles were observed, they still occurred in Atg5 deficient cells, implicating that they do not originate from an Atg5-dependent autophagic process.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Atg5-/- cells

claim: Depletion of host glycogen reduces luminal glycogen stores by no more than 20%
source: The observation that depletion of host glycogen (through silencing of the host glycogen synthase Gys1) reduces luminal glycogen stores by no more than 20% demonstrates that bulk uptake is a minor pathway for glycogen accumulation in the inclusion lumen.
evidence: This is calculated from the 82% remaining glycogen after Gys1 knockdown

claim: Bulk uptake is a minor pathway for glycogen accumulation in the inclusion lumen
source: The observation that depletion of host glycogen (through silencing of the host glycogen synthase Gys1) reduces luminal glycogen stores by no more than 20% demonstrates that bulk uptake is a minor pathway for glycogen accumulation in the inclusion lumen.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantification of glycogen after Gys1 knockdown

claim: De novo glycogen synthesis in the inclusion lumen is the main mechanism for luminal glycogen accumulation
source: The observation that depletion of host glycogen (through silencing of the host glycogen synthase Gys1) reduces luminal glycogen stores by no more than 20% demonstrates that bulk uptake is a minor pathway for glycogen accumulation in the inclusion lumen.
evidence: This is inferred from bulk uptake being minor, meaning de novo synthesis must be the major pathway

claim: Secretion of GlgX was not detected by an earlier study using mouse antisera
source: Secretion of GlgX, and of other enzymes involved in glycogen metabolism (except GlgA), was not detected by an earlier study using mouse antisera (Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous work

claim: GlgP localizes to the inclusion membrane
source: Interestingly, GlgP localization at the inclusion membrane was also reported (Saka et al., 2011), indicating that the two enzymes might work in concert, degrading host glycogen in the vicinity of the inclusion membrane.
evidence: This is cited from previous work

claim: GlgX and GlgP might work in concert, degrading host glycogen in the vicinity of the inclusion membrane
source: Interestingly, GlgP localization at the inclusion membrane was also reported (Saka et al., 2011), indicating that the two enzymes might work in concert, degrading host glycogen in the vicinity of the inclusion membrane.
evidence: This is speculated based on the co-localization of both enzymes at the inclusion membrane

claim: C. trachomatis uses T3S to transform the lumen of the inclusion into a glycogen storage compartment
source: Thus, altogether these data indicate that C. trachomatis uses T3S to transform the lumen of the inclusion into a glycogen storage compartment.
evidence: This is inferred from the T3S signals in glycogen metabolism enzymes and their secretion

claim: T3S is mostly described as a mechanism for protein translocation across a eukaryotic membrane
source: So far, T3S is mostly described as a mechanism for protein translocation across a eukaryotic membrane, either the plasma membrane or the membrane of a parasitophorous vacuole (Galan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation

claim: glgA transcription most likely controls the onset of glycogen synthesis
source: Our transcription analysis, in agreement with published data (Belland et al., 2003), indicates that glgA transcription most likely controls the onset of glycogen synthesis, as its initiation coincides with the onset of intraluminal glycogen accumulation (between 16 and 20 hpi).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between glgA transcription and glycogen appearance

claim: glgB is one of the few early genes
source: For all the other glycogen enzymes, transcription correlated with the known increase in bacterial metabolic activity between 8 and 24 hpi. The only other exception is glgB, which is one of the few early genes.
evidence: This is observed in the transcription analysis

claim: Defects in GlgA activity result in a loss of infectivity in vitro
source: These mutants demonstrated that defects in GlgA activity result in a loss of infectivity in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reduced progeny of GlgA mutants

claim: C. trachomatis GlgA can use both UDP-Glc and ADP-Glc as substrates
source: A zymogram analysis was performed to further compare chlamydial GlgA activity towards either UDP-Glc or ADP-Glc. Briefly, serial dilutions of lysates of E. coli lacking their endogenous glgA and transformed with either E. coli glgA or C. trachomatis glgA were separated on non-denaturing polyacrylamide gels that contained rabbit glycogen. The gels were subsequently incubated in buffer containing either UDP-Glc or ADP-Glc, and glycogen production was visualized by iodine staining. While E. coli GlgA showed activity exclusively upon incubation with ADP-Glc, as expected, the chlamydial GlgA showed activity with both substrates (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by zymogram analysis shown in Figure 5B
